unit.title: Develop and apply conversational skills in a foreign language

summary: This unit teaches you to use simple conversational Spanish with guests, and basic courtesy words in French and German: greetings for the time of day, polite forms of address, check-in and service phrases, directions, numbers, food and emergencies, what to do when you do not understand, and how to keep learning.

blocks.p: This unit teaches you to greet, help and serve guests in a language other than English. At Level 2 you will learn the **most useful phrases in Spanish**, and the basic courtesy words in **French and German**. You will also learn what to do when you do not understand a guest, and how to keep improving. It is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.

You are not expected to speak perfectly. You are expected to **try**, to be polite, to speak slowly and clearly, and to get help when you need it. A guest who hears 'Buenos días, bienvenidos' from a Jamaican receptionist feels welcome at once.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: two theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two practical tasks in the Centre. In the first you make a Spanish phrase card and act out welcome and check-in with a Spanish-speaking couple. In the second you make a courtesy poster in Spanish, French and German and serve a dinner for three guests who speak those languages. The assessor listens for correct words, a polite manner and what you do when stuck.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Spell words with their accents and question marks. 'Si' and 'sí' are different words, and 'ánimo' and 'animó' mean different things. Spanish questions begin with an upside-down mark: ¿Cómo se llama usted?
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Why languages matter and how to learn them

blocks.p: Jamaica welcomes visitors from the USA, Canada and the United Kingdom, and also from Europe, Latin America and elsewhere. Many are Spanish, French or German speakers, and some resorts and villas are owned by Spanish-speaking companies. When you greet guests in their own language:

ul: they feel **welcome and respected**
there are **fewer mistakes** with requests, orders and directions
guests write better reviews, return, and tell friends
you gain confidence, tips and chances of promotion

blocks.p: English spelling and Spanish spelling work differently. In the lists that follow, an approximate sound is shown in capital letters for the stressed part. Ask your instructor to say each word, and practise aloud.

head: Spanish letter
Sound
Example
rows: like the h in "hot", but stronger
z, and c before e or i
"s" in the Caribbean and Latin America

blocks.p: The **stress** (the loud part) is shown by an accent mark if the word breaks the usual rules: **días**, **habitación**, **teléfono**. The accent also separates words such as **tú** (you) and **tu** (your).

ul: Keep a **phrase card or notebook** for your job, and add one or two phrases each day.
Say new words **aloud**, often. Practise with a colleague, in the mirror or on a voice note.
Learn from guests and colleagues who speak the language. Ask 'How do you say ... ?'
Practise **role plays** at work, for example a check-in or a breakfast order.
Use apps, films, songs and the news in the language at home.
Ask about classes and training: HEART/NSTA Trust and TPDCo offer courses, and your Centre can advise you.
Use the language with real guests as soon as you are ready.

blocks.note: Many guests like to hear an effort, even if it is not perfect. A smile and 'Perdón, estoy aprendiendo español' (Sorry, I am learning Spanish) is welcome.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: In many languages there are two words for 'you': a **friendly** one for family, friends and children, and a **polite** one for people you do not know. At work, always use the polite form unless the guest invites you to use the friendly one.

head: Language
Friendly "you"
Polite "you"
rows: Sie (always written with a capital S)

blocks.p: In Spanish, 'usted' goes with the same verb form as 'he' or 'she': ¿**Cómo se llama usted**? (What is your name?) The question ¿Cómo te llamas? is the friendly one, for a child or a friend.

head: English
Spanish
French
German
rows: Frau (today most women are called Frau)

ul: Use the title and the **surname**: señor Pérez, Madame Dubois, Herr Schmidt, Frau Weber.
If you do not know the name, say simply 'señor' or 'señora' ('Sir' or 'Madam').
Let the guest tell you if they prefer the first name, then follow their lead.

In Spanish-speaking countries, many people have **two surnames** (for example, García Morales). The first is the father's name, the second is the mother's. When you write it on the form, copy both. Use the first surname with the title.

blocks.note: Good manners are about respect, not about perfect grammar. Always smile, look at the guest, and say 'please' and 'thank you' in their language.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Use 'usted' in every sentence you say to a guest: ¿Necesita usted algo? (Do you need something?). Do not use ¿Qué quieres? (What do you want?), which is too direct and friendly.

blocks.p: Write the room number on the key folder and show it to the guest, instead of saying it aloud where others can hear. You can also point to the number and say 'Su habitación es esta' (Your room is this one).

blocks.h: Words in the room and on the property

blocks.p: Guests often say what they want in short phrases: **Una toalla, por favor.** (A towel, please.) **La llave no funciona.** (The key does not work.) **No hay agua caliente.** (There is no hot water.) **El aire acondicionado no funciona.** (The air conditioner does not work.) When you hear a problem, say **'Lo siento. Enseguida lo arreglamos.'** (I am sorry. We will fix it right away.) and call maintenance.

head: Spanish
Meaning
rows: It is at the end of the corridor

blocks.p: Give a short sentence and point with an open hand (never with one finger): **'El restaurante está a la izquierda. Por aquí, por favor.'** If the place is far, offer to take the guest or to draw a map. After giving directions, ask '¿Entiende?' (Do you understand?), and smile.

sections.title: Numbers, days, times, food and emergencies

blocks.h: Numbers 1 to 10 and a few more

blocks.p: More Spanish numbers: once (11), doce (12), veinte (20), cien (100). Say prices, room numbers and times slowly, and write numbers down for the guest to confirm.
Spanish and French write the days with a small letter (martes, mardi); German writes them with a capital letter (Dienstag). 'Martes' is Tuesday and 'miércoles' is Wednesday.

ul: In Spain, Latin America, France and Germany, the date is written **day / month / year**. So 05/08 is the **5th of August**, not the 8th of May. The USA writes the month first, so always **confirm the date in words**.
Germany and much of Europe use the **24-hour clock**. A guest who says dinner is at '19:30' means 7:30 p.m. Write times in the same way when you confirm.
Time questions: ¿A qué hora es el desayuno? (What time is breakfast?) Answer: A las ocho. (At eight o'clock.)

head: Spanish
Meaning
rows: What would you like to drink?
el café / el té / la leche
The bill, please (the guest says this)

blocks.p: Take the order, **repeat it back**, and ask about allergies before the food goes to the kitchen. If you are not sure what a guest says, point to the menu and say '¿Esto?' (This one?).

blocks.note: In an emergency never delay help because of language. Call your supervisor, the first aider or the ambulance (110) at once, stay with the guest, use simple words and gestures, and ask a colleague or a translation app to help. Ask about allergies and medicines. In Jamaica the police are 119, and the ambulance and fire service are 110.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: At Level 2 you need the basic courtesy words in French and German. Learn them well, and use them with the polite form of 'you'.

ul: Say 'Bonjour' **before** any question or request. French guests expect it.
Use **Monsieur** or **Madame** with or without the surname: 'Bonjour, Madame Dubois.'
French has a space before ? and ! in writing. French has accents (é, è, ç): write them correctly.

head: German
Sounds like
Meaning
When
rows: Please / You are welcome / Here you are
Thank you / thank you very much

ul: Use **Herr** (Mr) and **Frau** (Mrs, Ms) with the surname: 'Guten Abend, Herr Schmidt.'
Use **Sie** for 'you' (with a capital S). Never use 'du' unless invited.
German nouns are written with a **capital letter**: das Zimmer, der Schlüssel, das Frühstück.
German guests are often **punctual**, and expect exact times and clear information. Write dates as 05.08 (day, month).

blocks.note: Pronunciation tip: in German, 'w' sounds like English 'v' and 'v' sounds like 'f'. In French, the final 's' and 't' in a word are usually silent.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Understanding each other and cultural awareness

flow: Say honestly that you did not understand

head: Situation
What to say or do
rows: You do not know the word
Un momento, por favor, and fetch a colleague
A serious matter (health, money, a complaint)
Never guess: get help from a supervisor or a trained translator

ul: Speak **slowly and clearly** with simple words. Do not shout or speak very loudly.
Avoid slang, jokes and fast Jamaican Patwa when speaking English to a guest who is learning it.
Use **gestures**, writing, numbers on paper, a map or pictures.
Use a translation app only to help, and check important points with a colleague.
Always check an order, a time or a price by repeating it back.

blocks.note: If you are not sure of the meaning, it is better to say 'I do not know. Let me find out' than to guess. Wrong guesses cause allergy problems, missed transfers and billing errors.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Customs differ between countries. Do not assume that all guests from one country are the same.
In Spain, lunch and dinner are often later than in Jamaica; Spanish and Latin American guests may ask for dinner at 9 or 10 p.m.
Many guests from Europe expect to be addressed by title and surname, and to be served with correct manners.
Handshakes are usual for a first greeting. Wait for the guest to offer a kiss or hug, which staff do not start.
Do not joke about a guest's country, accent or language. Never make guesses about nationality from a name or a skin colour.
Confirm **dates, times and prices in writing**.

blocks.p: Guests who speak Spanish may come from Spain, Cuba, Panama, Colombia, Mexico or other countries. Words and accents differ a little, but the phrases in this unit are understood everywhere.

blocks.note: When you serve a guest, your greeting, smile and eye contact say as much as your words. Keep a friendly, professional manner at all times.
blocks.label: Jamaica

c1.title: A Spanish-speaking couple arrives at a villa in Ocho Rios
c1.text: Mr Javier Torres and his wife Elena arrive at a villa property in Ocho Rios at 10:15 in the morning. They speak very little English. Receptionist Shanice has learned some Spanish and has a phrase card. The couple have a booking, and Mr Torres has his passport in his hand. After check-in, Mrs Torres asks '¿Dónde está la playa?' and Mr Torres tells Shanice that the key card does not work: 'La llave no funciona.'

c2.title: A Spanish-speaking family at breakfast
c2.text: At the villa restaurant, Andre serves a family from Panama at breakfast. The mother, Señora Castillo, says they would like 'dos cafés, un jugo y tres desayunos'. Her daughter, who is about 10, points to the menu and says 'alergia' while touching a picture of peanuts. The father asks for 'la cuenta' when they finish. Andre knows only a few Spanish words.

c3.title: French guests at a verandah dinner
c3.text: A French couple, Monsieur and Madame Lefèvre, are served dinner on the villa verandah at 7:45 p.m. Kerry-Ann, the server, greets them in French, brings water and a menu, and later puts the plates on the table. The couple thank her. At the end of the evening they say goodnight as they leave for their room.

c4.title: A German guest and the details
c4.text: Mr Klaus Becker, a guest from Germany, phones reception. He wants to book an airport transfer and says 'Ich möchte einen Transfer für den 12.08. um 14:30 Uhr.' Receptionist Rohan writes the information down. Mr Becker also says 'Danke' when Rohan confirms, and Rohan replies with a German phrase. Rohan is not sure whether the guest means the 8th of December.

c5.title: A guest in trouble at the pool
c5.text: One afternoon by the pool a Spanish-speaking guest, a man of about 60, suddenly holds his chest and sits down, looking pale. The only staff member nearby is poolside attendant Kimani, who speaks little Spanish. A colleague who speaks Spanish is at the other end of the property. Other guests are watching.

questions.q: It is 10:15 in the morning. Which greeting should Shanice use?
questions.why: Buenos días is the greeting from waking until about noon. Buenas tardes is for the afternoon, buenas noches for the evening, and hasta luego means 'see you later'.

questions.q: Shanice wants to ask the couple under what name the booking is made. Which phrase is correct?
questions.why: '¿A nombre de quién?' means 'Under what name?'. '¿Cuántas noches?' asks how many nights, and '¿Cómo está usted?' asks how you are.

questions.q: Which form of 'you' should Shanice use with Mr and Mrs Torres?
questions.why: Usted is the polite 'you' in Spanish. Tú is friendly and is not used with guests, while vous and du belong to French and German.

questions.q: Mrs Torres asks '¿Dónde está la playa?' What does she want to know?
questions.why: 'Playa' is the beach, 'piscina' is the pool, and 'restaurante' is the restaurant.

questions.q: Shanice says 'Lo siento. Enseguida lo arreglamos' about the key. What does she mean?
o: I am sorry. We will fix it right away
I do not understand. Please repeat it
One moment. Please wait at the door
Here is your new key. Enjoy your stay
questions.why: 'Lo siento' means 'I am sorry' and 'enseguida' means 'right away'. 'Arreglar' means to fix.

questions.q: Señora Castillo asks for 'dos cafés, un jugo y tres desayunos'. How many breakfasts should Andre bring?
questions.why: 'Tres' is three. 'Dos' is two and 'uno' (or 'un') is one.

questions.q: The daughter touches the picture of peanuts and says 'alergia'. What should Andre do?
o: Ignore it, because she is only a child and may be joking
Bring the dishes, and ask her to say if she feels ill after eating
Check the allergy with her parents, and tell the kitchen
Tell her to eat only the fruit and nothing else from the menu
questions.why: Allergy information must never be guessed or ignored. Check with the parents, using gestures or a colleague, and tell the kitchen before the food is prepared.

questions.q: The father says 'la cuenta'. What is he asking for?
questions.why: 'La cuenta' is the bill. 'La carta' is the menu and 'el baño' is the bathroom.

questions.q: As Andre puts the dishes on the table, which Spanish phrase wishes the family an enjoyable meal?
questions.why: 'Buen provecho' means 'Enjoy your meal' and is said when serving or to people who are eating. 'Hasta mañana' means 'see you tomorrow'.

questions.q: How should Kerry-Ann greet the Lefèvres at 7:45 p.m.?
questions.why: 'Bonsoir' is the French evening greeting. 'Bonne nuit' is only for bedtime, 'au revoir' is goodbye, and 'Guten Abend' is German.

questions.q: As she puts down the plates, Kerry-Ann wants to wish them an enjoyable meal in French. What does she say?
questions.why: 'Bon appétit' is said when serving food. 'Merci beaucoup' is thank you, 'bon séjour' is enjoy your stay and 'excusez-moi' is excuse me.

questions.q: Madame Lefèvre says 'Merci beaucoup'. What is the best reply?
questions.why: 'Je vous en prie' is a polite 'You are welcome'. 'S'il vous plaît' means please, and 'je ne comprends pas' means 'I do not understand'.

questions.q: The Lefèvres leave for the night. Which phrase is correct?
questions.why: 'Bonne nuit' is the French good night, said at bedtime. 'Bonjour' is a daytime greeting.

questions.q: Mr Becker says 'Ich möchte einen Transfer für den 12.08.' Which date is most likely?
questions.why: In Germany the date is written day, then month: 12.08 is 12 August. It is wise to confirm the date in words with the guest.

questions.q: Mr Becker says 14:30 Uhr. What time is that?
questions.why: On the 24-hour clock, 14:30 is 2:30 in the afternoon (14 - 12 = 2).

questions.q: Mr Becker says 'Danke'. What is a polite German reply from Rohan?
questions.why: 'Bitte' means 'you are welcome' in reply to danke. 'Willkommen' is welcome, 'Gute Nacht' is good night, and 'Entschuldigung' is excuse me.

questions.q: How should Rohan address Mr Becker on the phone?
o: Herr Becker, with the polite Sie
Mister Becker, with the French vous
questions.why: German guests are addressed with Herr or Frau and the surname, using Sie, the polite form.

questions.q: What is Kimani's first priority with the guest by the pool?
o: Wait until the Spanish-speaking colleague arrives before doing anything
Call for help at once, and stay with the guest
Ask the other guests to move away and leave the man alone to rest
Give him a drink of water and tell him to rest for an hour or so
questions.why: A possible heart problem is an emergency. Do not delay help because of language. Call for help (110 for the ambulance), stay calm and stay with the guest.

questions.q: Which Spanish question helps Kimani find out where it hurts?
questions.why: '¿Dónde le duele?' means 'Where does it hurt?'. The others ask where the bathroom is, how much something costs and whether the guest has a reservation.

questions.q: A guest speaks Spanish so fast that you cannot follow. Which phrase asks her politely to slow down?
questions.why: 'Más despacio, por favor' means 'More slowly, please'. 'Un momento' asks her to wait, and 'con permiso' is used to pass by. Do not pretend you understood.
